correctness.rationale: For n>=4, if the hub is a DFS root or leaf its incident tree cut contains n spokes and yields DTC>=n-1>=ceil(n/2)+1. Otherwise its strict ancestors are a contiguous rim path of length 1<=a<=n-1; the connected complementary rim path is wholly in the unique DFS child subtree of the hub. The incoming and outgoing hub tree cuts have a+2 and n-a+2 graph edges, so their crossing non-tree counts are a+1 and n-a+1, forcing the sharp lower bound. A Hamiltonian DFS path with a=floor(n/2) rim vertices before the hub has no enveloping arcs and its maximum cut-minus-one is exactly ceil(n/2)+1, proving KLX=DTC. The hub star shows ordinary spanning tree congestion 3, with the lower bound from 3-edge-connectivity; a four-vertex bag path decomposition and a K_4 minor show treewidth 3. A standalone contour-based verifier exhausts 2380 ordered DFS traversals for rim n=3..9 and separately checks the explicit construction through n=500. Finite tests are corroboration, not the infinite proof.

value.rationale: The theorem gives a natural infinite exact benchmark for the 2026 KLX parameter: all wheel graphs with n>=4 rim vertices, not an arbitrary finite slice. It shows an unbounded gap between depth-first traversal congestion ceil(n/2)+1 and classical spanning-tree congestion 3, even while the graphs remain planar, 3-connected, and have treewidth 3. The hub-cut bottleneck identifies why the DFS restriction has this cost and improves the general degree-based lower bound from nonsharp growth to a precise linear law. Both the crossing-only equality and attaining traversal have a clear algorithmic interpretation.
